passage: In the reading room of a university library in Prague, Marek spread five years of entrance papers across the table. Jana, studying beside him, watched him draw a chart with a ruler. "What is this?" she asked. "Every question, sorted by topic," he said. Marek added them up. Algebra and probability together took nearly half of all marks every year. Poetry analysis, a topic he loved, was worth very little. "So the first month goes to algebra and probability," he said. "The rare topics wait." Jana raised an eyebrow. "You love poetry." "I know," said Marek, "and I will get to it. Just not first." He wrote "Week 1: algebra" at the top of a fresh page.

qa.q: Which two topics took nearly half of the marks every year?
qa.a: Algebra and probability took nearly half of all marks every year.

qa.q: What is Marek feeling about putting poetry analysis last?
qa.a: Marek feels a little reluctant but resolved, admitting he loves poetry yet choosing to start elsewhere.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Marek add to the marks chart, and why?
qa.a: He could also check which topics he finds hardest, because marks show value but a weak spot in a high-marks topic needs more time.

qa.q: How does Jana see Marek's plan?
qa.a: Jana is surprised, raising an eyebrow and pointing out that Marek loves poetry, so Jana sees the sacrifice in the plan.

grounding: Shows prioritising study topics by analysing which subjects carry more marks in past papers, and postponing the rarely tested ones.
